/-!
# Meyniel's conjecture on the cop number

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Cop number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cop_number)
- [Bonato and Prałat, *Meyniel's conjecture on the cop number: a survey*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.3385)
-/

universe u

namespace CopNumber

/-- A move in the cops-and-robber game is legal if it follows an edge or stays at the current
vertex. -/
def IsLegalMove {V : Type u} (G : SimpleGraph V) (v w : V) : Prop :=
  v = w ∨ G.Adj v w

/-- A position of the game with `k` cops records every cop's vertex and the robber's vertex. -/
abbrev Position (V : Type u) (k : ℕ) := (Fin k → V) × V

/-- A cop strategy chooses the cops' next simultaneous move from the finite history of positions.
Its subtype condition says that every cop either follows an edge or passes. -/
def CopsStrategy {V : Type u} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) :=
  ∀ (t : ℕ) (history : Fin (t + 1) → Position V k),
    {next : Fin k → V //
      ∀ i, IsLegalMove G ((history (Fin.last t)).1 i) (next i)}

/-- `CopsWin G k` means that `k` cops have a winning strategy on `G`. The cops choose their
initial vertices before the robber chooses his. Thereafter the cops and robber alternate, with the
cops moving first; either side may pass. The two alternatives in the capture condition detect
capture after a robber move (including initial placement) and after a cop move, respectively. -/
def CopsWin {V : Type u} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (initial : Fin k → V) (strategy : CopsStrategy G k),
    ∀ (cops : ℕ → Fin k → V) (robber : ℕ → V),
      cops 0 = initial →
      (∀ t, cops (t + 1) =
        (strategy t (fun j => (cops j, robber j))).1) →
      (∀ t, IsLegalMove G (robber t) (robber (t + 1))) →
      ∃ t, (∃ i, cops t i = robber t) ∨ (∃ i, cops (t + 1) i = robber t)

/-- The cop number of a finite graph is the least number of cops having a winning strategy. -/
noncomputable def copNumber {V : Type u} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k : ℕ | CopsWin G k}

/--
**Meyniel's conjecture.** There is a constant $d>0$, independent of the graph, such that every
connected finite simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices has cop number at most $d\sqrt n$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem cop_number :
    ∃ d : ℝ, 0 < d ∧
      ∀ {V : Type u} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V), G.Connected →
        (copNumber G : ℝ) ≤ d * Real.sqrt (Fintype.card V) := by
  sorry

end CopNumber
modeling_decisions: Interpreted the terse list entry using the linked Cop number article and Bonato–Prałat survey: one constant d > 0 bounds every connected finite simple graph G by copNumber G ≤ d * sqrt(|V(G)|).
Represented the standard reflexive-game convention on Mathlib's irreflexive SimpleGraph by declaring a move legal when it follows an edge or leaves the piece at the same vertex.
Indexed recorded positions immediately after robber placements/moves. Consequently, the winning condition checks capture both at a recorded position and immediately after the next cop move.

Modeled a deterministic perfect-information cop strategy as a function of the finite position history. Its output is a subtype carrying legality of every cop's simultaneous move, which prevents illegal strategies from winning vacuously.

Quantified over all infinite legal robber trajectories rather than explicit robber strategies. Against a fixed history-dependent cop strategy these describe exactly all possible robber choices, while finite capture is expressed by an existential time.
Defined the cop number as the natural-number infimum of the set of k for which the cops have a winning strategy. The conjecture only applies to connected graphs, whose vertex types are nonempty.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Cop number: Meyniel's conjecture

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Cop number*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cop_number)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [W. Baird, A. Bonato, *Meyniel's conjecture on the cop number: a survey*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.3385)

*Cops and Robbers* is a perfect-information pursuit-evasion game played on a graph $G$ by a
player controlling $k$ cops and a player controlling a single robber.
- First the cops are placed on vertices of $G$ (several cops may share a vertex), then the robber
  is placed on a vertex of $G$.
- Afterwards the players alternate turns, the cops moving first. On the cops' turn every cop
  either stays put or moves to an adjacent vertex. On the robber's turn the robber either stays
  put or moves to an adjacent vertex.
- The cops win as soon as a cop occupies the same vertex as the robber (a *capture*). The robber
  wins if this never happens.

The *cop number* $c(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $k$ cops have a winning strategy on $G$.

**Meyniel's conjecture** (1985) states that $c(G) = O(\sqrt{n})$ for connected graphs $G$ on $n$
vertices.

In this file the game is formalised through strategies of the cops. Because the cops' strategy is
deterministic and the robber has full information, quantifying over all *strategies* of the robber
is the same as quantifying over all legal *walks* of the robber, which is what we do.
-/

namespace CopNumber

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V)

/-- A token standing on the vertex `u` of `G` can move to `v` in one turn if it either stays put
(`v = u`) or moves along an edge of `G`. -/
def IsMove (u v : V) : Prop := u = v ∨ G.Adj u v

/-- A sequence of vertices `p 0, p 1, p 2, …` is a legal walk on `G` if each step is a legal
move, i.e. a token can follow it moving at most one edge per turn. -/
def IsLegalWalk (p : ℕ → V) : Prop := ∀ n, IsMove G (p n) (p (n + 1))

/-- A strategy for `k` cops on the vertex set `V`. Since the game has perfect information, the
cops' positions at time `n` may depend on the whole history of the game, which is determined by
the robber's positions at times `0, …, n - 1`. Thus `σ n h` is the vector of cop positions at
time `n` when the robber has occupied the vertices `h 0, …, h (n - 1)` so far. In particular
`σ 0` is the initial placement of the cops, chosen before the robber is placed. -/
def CopStrategy (V : Type*) (k : ℕ) := (n : ℕ) → (Fin n → V) → Fin k → V

variable {k : ℕ}

/-- The positions of the cops at time `n` when they follow the strategy `σ` and the robber
occupies the vertex `r m` at time `m`. -/
def CopStrategy.positions (σ : CopStrategy V k) (r : ℕ → V) (n : ℕ) : Fin k → V :=
  σ n fun j => r j

/-- The strategy `σ` is legal on `G`: whatever legal walk the robber follows, every cop follows a
legal walk of `G`, i.e. at each turn it stays put or moves along an edge. -/
def CopStrategy.IsLegal (σ : CopStrategy V k) : Prop :=
  ∀ r : ℕ → V, IsLegalWalk G r → ∀ i, IsLegalWalk G fun n => σ.positions r n i

/-- The strategy `σ` is winning for the cops on `G`: whatever legal walk the robber follows, at
some time some cop occupies the vertex of the robber. Here `r n` is the position of the robber at
time `n`; the capture occurs either after the cops' move at time `n + 1`, while the robber is still
at `r n`, or with the cops at their time-`n` positions (this includes the robber being placed on a
cop at time `0`, or moving onto a cop). -/
def CopStrategy.IsWinning (σ : CopStrategy V k) : Prop :=
  ∀ r : ℕ → V, IsLegalWalk G r →
    ∃ n i, σ.positions r n i = r n ∨ σ.positions r (n + 1) i = r n

/-- `k` cops can win the game of Cops and Robbers on `G`: there is a legal winning strategy for
`k` cops. -/
def CopsWin (k : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ σ : CopStrategy V k, σ.IsLegal G ∧ σ.IsWinning G

/-- The cop number $c(G)$ of `G`: the least number `k` of cops that can win the game of Cops and
Robbers on `G`. On a finite graph one cop per vertex always wins, so this is well defined; the
junk value `sInf ∅ = 0` only arises for infinite graphs on which no finite number of cops wins. -/
noncomputable def copNumber : ℕ := sInf {k | CopsWin G k}

/-- Placing one cop on every vertex wins immediately. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copsWin_card [Fintype V] : CopsWin G (Fintype.card V) := by
  refine ⟨fun _ _ => (Fintype.equivFin V).symm, fun r _ i n => Or.inl rfl, fun r _ => ?_⟩
  exact ⟨0, Fintype.equivFin V (r 0), Or.inl (by simp [CopStrategy.positions])⟩

/-- With no cops at all, the robber can never be captured. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem not_copsWin_zero [Nonempty V] : ¬ CopsWin G 0 := by
  rintro ⟨σ, -, hσ⟩
  obtain ⟨_, i, -⟩ := hσ (fun _ => Classical.arbitrary V) fun _ => Or.inl rfl
  exact i.elim0

/-- The cop number of a finite graph is at most its number of vertices. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_le_card [Fintype V] : copNumber G ≤ Fintype.card V :=
  Nat.sInf_le (copsWin_card G)

/-- The cop number of a nonempty finite graph is positive. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_pos [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] : 0 < copNumber G := by
  have h : copNumber G ∈ {k | CopsWin G k} := Nat.sInf_mem ⟨_, copsWin_card G⟩
  exact Nat.pos_of_ne_zero fun h0 => not_copsWin_zero G (h0 ▸ h)

/-- On a complete graph a single cop wins in one move. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_top [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] : copNumber (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) = 1 := by
  refine le_antisymm (Nat.sInf_le ?_) (copNumber_pos _)
  -- The cop starts anywhere and then always moves onto the robber's current vertex.
  let σ : CopStrategy V 1 := fun n => match n with
    | 0 => fun _ _ => Classical.arbitrary V
    | n + 1 => fun h _ => h (Fin.last n)
  have hpos (r : ℕ → V) (n : ℕ) (i : Fin 1) : σ.positions r (n + 1) i = r n := rfl
  refine ⟨σ, fun r _ i n => ?_, fun r _ => ⟨0, 0, Or.inr (hpos r 0 0)⟩⟩
  by_cases h : σ.positions r n i = σ.positions r (n + 1) i
  · exact Or.inl h
  · exact Or.inr h

/-- On two isolated vertices a single cop never catches the robber: the robber sits on the vertex
not occupied by the cop, and the cop cannot move. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 91]
theorem not_copsWin_bot_one : ¬ CopsWin (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) 1 := by
  rintro ⟨σ, hleg, hwin⟩
  let r : ℕ → Fin 2 := fun _ => σ 0 Fin.elim0 0 + 1
  have hr : IsLegalWalk ⊥ r := fun _ => Or.inl rfl
  have hc : ∀ n, σ.positions r n 0 = σ 0 Fin.elim0 0 := by
    intro n
    induction n with
    | zero => simp only [CopStrategy.positions]; rw [Subsingleton.elim (fun _ => _) Fin.elim0]
    | succ n ih =>
      rcases hleg r hr 0 n with h | h
      · exact (show σ.positions r n 0 = σ.positions r (n + 1) 0 from h) ▸ ih
      · exact ((SimpleGraph.bot_adj _ _).mp h).elim
  obtain ⟨n, i, h | h⟩ := hwin r hr
  · rw [Fin.fin_one_eq_zero i, hc n] at h
    exact absurd h (by simp [r])
  · rw [Fin.fin_one_eq_zero i, hc (n + 1)] at h
    exact absurd h (by simp [r])

/-- The cop number of the graph with two isolated vertices is `2`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_bot_fin_two : copNumber (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) = 2 := by
  refine le_antisymm (by simpa using copNumber_le_card (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)))
    (le_csInf ⟨_, copsWin_card _⟩ fun k hk => ?_)
  by_contra hlt
  interval_cases k
  · exact not_copsWin_zero _ hk
  · exact not_copsWin_bot_one hk

/-- **Meyniel's conjecture** (communicated to Frankl in 1985): the cop number of a connected graph
on $n$ vertices is $O(\sqrt{n})$. That is, there is a constant $d > 0$ such that every finite
connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices satisfies $c(G) \le d \sqrt{n}$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 5 91]
theorem cop_number :
    ∃ d : ℝ, 0 < d ∧ ∀ (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V), G.Connected →
      (copNumber G : ℝ) ≤ d * √(Fintype.card V) := by
  sorry

end CopNumber

modeling_decisions: Big-O reading: the terse list entry 'cop number is O(√n)' is stated, following the article and the Baird–Bonato survey, as ∃ d > 0 such that every finite connected graph G on n vertices has c(G) ≤ d·√n, with d chosen before the graph. This is equivalent to c(n) = O(√n) for the max function c(n) (finitely many graphs per n, each with finite cop number, so 'for n sufficiently large' can be absorbed into d); an explicit constant was preferred over Asymptotics.IsBigO on a max-over-graphs function for transparency.

Robber modelled as an arbitrary legal walk r : ℕ → V rather than a history-dependent strategy: since the cops' strategy is deterministic and the robber has perfect information, every robber strategy against σ produces a legal walk and every legal walk is realised by a (history-independent) robber strategy; so 'σ beats every robber strategy' ⟺ 'σ beats every legal walk'. Cop strategies are fully history-dependent (they see the robber's whole history; their own history is determined), so no positional/memoryless restriction or finiteness assumption is needed for faithfulness.

Capture condition includes both 'cop moves onto robber' (c (n+1) i = r n) and 'robber occupies a cop's vertex' (c n i = r n, covering the robber placing himself on a cop at time 0 or moving onto a cop), matching 'the cops win whenever the robber occupies the same vertex as a cop'.
Cop legality is required for all times against every legal robber walk (including after a capture); this does not change which k win, since cops can always stay put.

Connectedness is imposed via Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.Connected` (which includes `Nonempty V`), and finiteness via `[Fintype V]`; the constant `0 < d` is included as in the survey (redundant but harmless). Graphs are quantified over all vertex types `V : Type*` with a `Fintype` instance rather than only `Fin n`.

copNumber takes the junk value 0 (sInf ∅) only for infinite graphs where no finite number of cops wins; irrelevant to the conjecture, which quantifies over finite graphs where `copNumber_le_card` and `copNumber_pos` are proven.

Sanity tests included: cop number of a complete graph is 1, one cop per vertex always wins, zero cops never win on a nonempty graph, and the robber wins against one cop on two isolated vertices (cop number 2), checking that neither side of the game is vacuous.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Cop number

The *cop number* $c(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the least number of cops that suffices to capture a
robber in the game of Cops and Robbers on $G$. The rules of the game are:

* First the cops are placed on vertices of $G$ (several cops may share a vertex).
* Then the robber is placed on a vertex of $G$.
* The players then alternate turns, the cops moving first. On the cops' turn every cop either
  stays put or moves to an adjacent vertex. On the robber's turn the robber either stays put or
  moves to an adjacent vertex.
* The cops win as soon as a cop and the robber occupy the same vertex (a *capture*). The robber
  wins by evading capture forever.

Meyniel's conjecture (1985) states that every connected graph on $n$ vertices has cop number
$O(\sqrt{n})$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Cop number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cop_number)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- W. Baird, A. Bonato, *Meyniel's conjecture on the cop number: a survey*,
  Journal of Combinatorics 3 (2012), 225–238. [arXiv:1308.3385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.3385)
- P. Frankl, *Cops and robbers in graphs with large girth and Cayley graphs*,
  Discrete Applied Mathematics 17 (1987), 301–305.
-/

namespace CopNumber

variable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V)

/-- The positions of the game of Cops and Robbers with `k` cops on `G` from which the cops can
force a capture in finitely many rounds.

`CopsWin G true c r` means that the cops occupy the vertices `c 0, …, c (k - 1)`, the robber
occupies `r`, it is the cops' turn to move, and the cops can force a capture.
`CopsWin G false c r` is the same, but with the robber to move.

In a turn, each player either stays put or moves to an adjacent vertex, i.e. moves along the
reflexive closure `Relation.ReflGen G.Adj` of the adjacency relation. On the cops' turn every cop
moves independently, so any subset of the cops may move while the others stay put. A capture
happens as soon as a cop and the robber share a vertex. -/
inductive CopsWin {k : ℕ} : Bool → (Fin k → V) → V → Prop
  | capture (turn : Bool) (c : Fin k → V) (r : V) (h : ∃ i, c i = r) : CopsWin turn c r
  | copsMove (c : Fin k → V) (r : V) (c' : Fin k → V)
      (hc : ∀ i, Relation.ReflGen G.Adj (c i) (c' i)) (h : CopsWin false c' r) : CopsWin true c r
  | robberMove (c : Fin k → V) (r : V)
      (h : ∀ r', Relation.ReflGen G.Adj r r' → CopsWin true c r') : CopsWin false c r

/-- The cop number of `G`: the least number `k` of cops that have a winning strategy in Cops and
Robbers on `G`. That is, the least `k` such that `k` cops can be placed on `G` so that, wherever
the robber then places himself, the cops (moving first) can force a capture.

For a finite nonempty graph placing a cop on every vertex wins, so the set is nonempty and
`copNumber G` is a genuine minimum. -/
noncomputable def copNumber : ℕ :=
  sInf {k : ℕ | ∃ c : Fin k → V, ∀ r : V, CopsWin G true c r}

/-- Without any cops the robber is never captured. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem not_copsWin_zero {turn : Bool} {c : Fin 0 → V} {r : V} : ¬ CopsWin G turn c r := by
  intro h
  induction h with
  | capture _ _ _ h => exact h.choose.elim0
  | copsMove _ _ _ _ _ ih => exact ih
  | robberMove _ r _ ih => exact ih r .refl

/-- Placing a cop on every vertex wins immediately. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_le_card [Fintype V] : copNumber G ≤ Fintype.card V :=
  Nat.sInf_le ⟨fun i => (Fintype.equivFin V).symm i, fun r =>
    .capture _ _ _ ⟨Fintype.equivFin V r, by simp⟩⟩

/-- A nonempty finite graph needs at least one cop. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_pos [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] : 0 < copNumber G := by
  refine Nat.pos_of_ne_zero fun h => ?_

def IsCapture {V : Type*} {k : ℕ} (cops : CopsPosition V k) (robber : V) : Prop :=
  ∃ i, cops i = robber

/--
A cop strategy chooses the cops' next positions from the finite chronological history of
positions after robber turns. It is legal if every cop moves along one edge or stays put.
Requiring legality on every nonempty history prevents an illegal move from counting as a win.
-/
def IsLegalCopStrategy {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ}
    (strategy : List (GamePosition V k) → CopsPosition V k) : Prop :=
  ∀ (history : List (GamePosition V k)) (cops : CopsPosition V k) (robber : V),
    history.getLast? = some (cops, robber) →
      ∀ i, MayMove G (cops i) (strategy history i)

An infinite evading play starts after the cops place themselves and the robber then chooses a
vertex. In every later round the cops move first according to their strategy, and then the
robber moves. Both may stay put. The two non-capture conditions check capture immediately after
the cops' move and after the robber's move, respectively.
-/
def IsEvadingPlay {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ}
    (initial : CopsPosition V k)
    (strategy : List (GamePosition V k) → CopsPosition V k)
    (play : ℕ → GamePosition V k) : Prop :=
  (play 0).1 = initial ∧
  (∀ n, ¬ IsCapture (play n).1 (play n).2) ∧
  ∀ n,
    let nextCops := strategy ((List.range (n + 1)).map play)

robber can make legal moves and evade capture forever.

  ∃ (initial : CopsPosition V k)

    ¬ ∃ play : ℕ → GamePosition V k, IsEvadingPlay G initial strategy play

on their turn the cops move each cop to an adjacent vertex or leave it in place, and on his turn
the robber moves to an adjacent vertex or stays put. The cops win when the robber occupies the
same vertex as a cop (a *capture*); the robber wins if he evades capture forever.

The *cop number* $c(G)$ of `G` is the least `k` such that `k` cops have a winning strategy on `G`.

**Meyniel's conjecture** (1985) states that the cop number of a connected graph on $n$ vertices is
$O(\sqrt n)$: there is a constant $d > 0$ such that $c(G) \le d\sqrt{n}$ for every connected
graph $G$ on $n$ vertices.

namespace CopNumber

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ}

/-- `IsStep G v w` means that a player standing at `v` may end its turn at `w`:
it either stays put or moves along an edge of `G`. -/
def IsStep (v w : V) : Prop := v = w ∨ G.Adj v w

/-- `IsCopsMove G c c'` means that the cops may move from the configuration `c` to the
configuration `c'`: each cop either stays put or moves to an adjacent vertex.
Cops are indexed by `Fin k`, so several cops may occupy the same vertex. -/
def IsCopsMove (c c' : Fin k → V) : Prop := ∀ i, IsStep G (c i) (c' i)

/-- `IsCopsWinPosition G c r` means that the cops, standing at `c`, can force the capture of the
robber, standing at `r`, when it is the robber's turn to move. This is the least predicate such
that
* the cops win if the robber is already captured, i.e. some cop stands on `r`;
* the cops win if for every move `r'` of the robber they have a response `f r'` after which they
  still win. -/
inductive IsCopsWinPosition : (Fin k → V) → V → Prop
  | capture {c : Fin k → V} {r : V} (h : ∃ i, c i = r) : IsCopsWinPosition c r
  | step {c : Fin k → V} {r : V} (f : V → Fin k → V)
      (hf : ∀ r', IsStep G r r' → IsCopsMove G c (f r'))
      (h : ∀ r', IsStep G r r' → IsCopsWinPosition (f r') r') :
      IsCopsWinPosition c r

/-- `CopsWin G k` means that `k` cops have a winning strategy on `G`: the cops can choose their
initial configuration `c` so that, wherever the robber then chooses to start, the cops have a
first move `c'` after which they can force a capture. -/
def CopsWin (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ c : Fin k → V, ∀ r : V, ∃ c', IsCopsMove G c c' ∧ IsCopsWinPosition G c' r

/-- The cop number of `G`: the least number of cops that have a winning strategy on `G`.
For a finite graph this is a well-defined natural number, since placing a cop on every vertex
wins. (If no finite number of cops wins, which can only happen for infinite graphs, the
convention `sInf ∅ = 0` applies.) -/
noncomputable def copNumber : ℕ := sInf {k | CopsWin G k}

/-- The robber is never captured when there are no cops. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem not_isCopsWinPosition_zero (c : Fin 0 → V) (r : V) : ¬ IsCopsWinPosition G c r := by
  intro h
  induction h with
  | capture h => exact h.elim fun i _ => i.elim0
  | step _ _ _ ih => exact ih _ (Or.inl rfl)

/-- Zero cops never win on a nonempty graph. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem not_copsWin_zero [Nonempty V] : ¬ CopsWin G 0 := by
  rintro ⟨c, hc⟩
  obtain ⟨c', -, h⟩ := hc (Classical.arbitrary V)
  exact not_isCopsWinPosition_zero G c' _ h

/-- Placing a cop on every vertex wins. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copsWin_card [Fintype V] : CopsWin G (Fintype.card V) :=
  ⟨(Fintype.equivFin V).symm, fun r => ⟨_, fun _ => Or.inl rfl,
    .capture ⟨Fintype.equivFin V r, (Fintype.equivFin V).symm_apply_apply r⟩⟩⟩

/-- The cop number of a finite graph is at most its number of vertices. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_le_card [Fintype V] : copNumber G ≤ Fintype.card V :=
  Nat.sInf_le (copsWin_card G)

/-- The cop number of a nonempty finite graph is positive. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_pos [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] : 0 < copNumber G := by
  rw [Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero]
  intro h
  rw [copNumber, Nat.sInf_eq_zero] at h
  rcases h with h | h
  · exact not_copsWin_zero G h
  · exact h.subset (copsWin_card G)

/-- The cop number of a nonempty complete graph is one: a single cop captures the robber
in the first round. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_top [Nonempty V] : copNumber (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) = 1 := by
  refine IsLeast.csInf_eq ⟨⟨fun _ => Classical.arbitrary V, fun r => ⟨fun _ => r, fun _ => ?_,
    .capture ⟨0, rfl⟩⟩⟩, fun k hk => ?_⟩
  · by_cases h : Classical.arbitrary V = r
    · exact Or.inl h
    · exact Or.inr h
  · exact Nat.pos_of_ne_zero fun h => not_copsWin_zero _ (h ▸ hk)

@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem isStep_cycleGraph_four {x y : Fin 4} (h : IsStep (cycleGraph 4) x y) : y ≠ x + 2 := by
  unfold IsStep at h
  rw [cycleGraph_adj (n := 2)] at h
  revert x y; decide

/-- On the cycle `C₄`, a player not standing at `x` may step to the vertex opposite to `x`. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem isStep_cycleGraph_four_add_two {x y : Fin 4} (h : x ≠ y) :
    IsStep (cycleGraph 4) y (x + 2) := by
  unfold IsStep
  rw [cycleGraph_adj (n := 2)]
  revert x y; decide

/-- On the cycle `C₄`, a robber not standing on the single cop can evade capture forever
by always moving to the vertex opposite to the cop. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem not_isCopsWinPosition_cycleGraph_four {c : Fin 1 → Fin 4} {r : Fin 4} (hcr : c 0 ≠ r) :
    ¬ IsCopsWinPosition (cycleGraph 4) c r := by
  intro h
  induction h with
  | capture h =>
    obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := h
    exact hcr (Fin.fin_one_eq_zero i ▸ hi)
  | step _ hf _ ih =>
    have hstep := isStep_cycleGraph_four_add_two hcr
    exact ih _ hstep (isStep_cycleGraph_four (hf _ hstep 0))

/-- A single cop does not win on the cycle `C₄`. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 91]
theorem not_copsWin_cycleGraph_four_one : ¬ CopsWin (cycleGraph 4) 1 := by
  rintro ⟨c, hc⟩
  obtain ⟨c', hmove, h⟩ := hc (c 0 + 2)
  exact not_isCopsWinPosition_cycleGraph_four (isStep_cycleGraph_four (hmove 0)) h

then captures the robber in the first round. -/

  refine ⟨![0, 2], fun r => ⟨![if r = 2 then 0 else r, 2], fun i => ?_, .capture ?_⟩⟩
  · unfold IsStep
    rw [cycleGraph_adj (n := 2)]
    revert i r; decide
  · by_cases hr : r = 2
    · exact ⟨1, by simp [hr]⟩
    · exact ⟨0, by simp [hr]⟩

/-- The cop number of the cycle `C₄` is two. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 91]
theorem copNumber_cycleGraph_four : copNumber (cycleGraph 4) = 2 := by
  refine IsLeast.csInf_eq ⟨copsWin_cycleGraph_four_two, fun k hk => ?_⟩
  rcases k with _ | _ | k
  · exact (not_copsWin_zero _ hk).elim
  · exact (not_copsWin_cycleGraph_four_one hk).elim
  · omega

    ∃ d : ℝ, 0 < d ∧ ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), G.Connected →

end CopNumber

# Cop number

The game of *Cops and Robbers* is played on a finite graph $G$ by a set of $k$ cops and a
single robber, who occupy vertices of $G$. First the cops are placed on vertices of $G$ (several
cops may share a vertex), then the robber is placed on a vertex. Afterwards the players alternate
turns, cops first. On the cops' turn each cop either stays put or moves to an adjacent vertex; on
the robber's turn the robber either stays put or moves to an adjacent vertex. The cops win if,
after finitely many rounds, some cop occupies the same vertex as the robber; otherwise the
robber wins. The *cop number* $c(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $k$ cops have a winning
strategy on $G$.

**Meyniel's conjecture** (1985, reported by Frankl) states that the cop number of every
connected $n$-vertex graph is $O(\sqrt n)$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Cop number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cop_number)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)

  Journal of Combinatorics 3 (2012), 225–238. [arXiv:1308.3385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.3385)
- [Fra87] P. Frankl, *Cops and robbers in graphs with large girth and Cayley graphs*,

-/

namespace CopNumber

variable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V)

/--

the vertices `c 0, …, c (k - 1)`, the robber standing on `r`, and the cops to move, the cops can
force a capture in finitely many rounds.

On their turn the cops move to positions `c'`, where each cop either stays put or moves to an
adjacent vertex. If some cop now stands on the robber's vertex, the robber is captured. Otherwise
the robber either stays put or moves to an adjacent vertex `r'`, and the cops must be able to
force a capture from the position `(c', r')`.
-/
inductive CopsWin {k : ℕ} : (Fin k → V) → V → Prop
  /-- The cops move to `c'` and one of them lands on the robber. -/
  | capture {c : Fin k → V} {r : V} (c' : Fin k → V)
      (hc' : ∀ i, c' i = c i ∨ G.Adj (c i) (c' i)) (h : ∃ i, c' i = r) :
      CopsWin c r
  /-- The cops move to `c'`, and whatever the robber does next, the cops can still force a
  capture. -/
  | step {c : Fin k → V} {r : V} (c' : Fin k → V)
      (hc' : ∀ i, c' i = c i ∨ G.Adj (c i) (c' i))
      (h : ∀ r', (r' = r ∨ G.Adj r r') → CopsWin c' r') :
      CopsWin c r

`k` cops have a winning strategy on `G`: the cops can be placed on vertices `c 0, …, c (k - 1)`
of `G` (repetitions allowed) so that, wherever the robber then places himself, the cops can
force a capture.
-/
def CopsCanWin (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ c : Fin k → V, ∀ r : V, CopsWin G c r

  rw [h0] at hmem
